You’re wrong about how the Affordable Care Act actually works. ACA subsidies do not get funneled to insurance companies as some kind of giveaway, they go to insured people to reduce what they pay in premiums and out of pocket costs. Insurers cannot simply pocket that money. If premiums rise, the subsidy rises to protect the consumer, not to boost corporate profits.

You’re also ignoring the ACA’s medical loss ratio rules, which legally require insurers in the individual market to spend at least 80 percent of premium dollars on actual medical care. If they fail to do that, they must issue rebates to consumers. That is not “ripping off taxpayers,” it is one of the tightest spending constraints in the entire U.S. insurance system, far stricter than what exists in most employer plans that are also subsidized through the tax code.

High deductibles are not proof the ACA “broke” healthcare. They are the result of plan design choices and cost control strategies that predate the ACA and are common across the entire insurance market. In fact, the ACA reduced deductibles and out of pocket costs for millions through cost sharing reductions. Letting subsidies expire would increase deductibles and premiums at the same time for the people you claim to be standing up for.

Letting the enhanced subsidies expire would not “fix healthcare,” it would immediately cause premiums to spike, often doubling or tripling for working families, early retirees, and small business owners. Many would drop coverage altogether. That does not hurt insurance companies, it shrinks the risk pool, drives premiums higher for those who remain insured, and increases uncompensated care that taxpayers ultimately pay for anyway.

The COVID era subsidies you want to kill didn’t enrich insurers, they capped premiums as a share of income and eliminated the subsidy cliff. That is why enrollment hit record highs and the uninsured rate fell. Ending them reverses those gains and hands insurers more leverage in a smaller, sicker market.

If your real goal were to stop insurance companies from profiting, you’d be talking about stronger competition, tougher rate review, and enforcing spending rules, not pulling subsidies away from patients. Saying “just say NO” doesn’t punish insurers, it punishes people who rely on coverage and makes the system more expensive for everyone.
